questions.prompt: A patient presents with acute dyspnoea and bilateral crackles. Which investigation best confirms cardiogenic pulmonary oedema at the bedside?

options.text: Bedside lung ultrasound showing diffuse B-lines

rationales.a: Diffuse bilateral B-lines indicate interstitial oedema and are obtainable in minutes.
rationales.b: Troponin rises in many conditions and does not confirm oedema.
rationales.c: Holter assesses rhythm over time, not acute fluid status.
rationales.d: Exercise testing is contraindicated during acute decompensation.

questions.explanation: Lung ultrasound is the fastest bedside confirmation of interstitial oedema.

questions.prompt: Which of the following reduce cardiac preload?

rationales.a: Venodilation reduces venous return, lowering preload.
rationales.b: Diuresis reduces circulating volume, lowering preload.
rationales.c: An alpha-1 agonist; raises afterload rather than reducing preload.
rationales.d: A vasopressor — raises filling pressures rather than lowering them.
rationales.e: An inotrope; increases contractility without reducing preload.

questions.explanation: Preload is venous return. Venodilators and diuretics lower it; vasopressors raise it.

questions.prompt: In cardiogenic shock with a systolic pressure of 70 mmHg, which agent is the most appropriate first-line vasopressor?

rationales.a: Restores perfusion pressure with less tachyarrhythmia than dopamine.
rationales.b: Diuresis in a hypotensive patient worsens shock.
rationales.c: Venodilation would drop an already inadequate pressure further.
rationales.d: Beta blockade is harmful in decompensated shock.

questions.explanation: Perfusion pressure comes first; diuresis and vasodilation come after stabilisation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are recognised adverse effects of long-term loop diuretic therapy?

rationales.a: Increased distal sodium delivery drives potassium loss.
rationales.b: Dose-related, particularly with rapid intravenous administration.
rationales.c: Loop diuretics lower potassium; potassium-sparing agents raise it.
rationales.d: Diuresis causes weight loss, not gain.
rationales.e: Not a recognised effect of loop diuretics.

questions.explanation: Two classics worth holding on to: potassium loss and ototoxicity.

questions.prompt: Which laboratory finding most strongly suggests acute digoxin toxicity?

rationales.a: Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition raises extracellular potassium and slows conduction.
rationales.b: Points to hepatobiliary disease, not digoxin.

questions.explanation: Acute digoxin toxicity raises potassium — the opposite of what most people expect.

questions.prompt: Which of the following interactions meaningfully increase serum digoxin levels?

rationales.a: Reduces renal and non-renal clearance; the digoxin dose is usually halved.
rationales.c: A P-glycoprotein inducer, so it lowers digoxin levels.
rationales.e: Binds digoxin in the gut and reduces absorption.

questions.explanation: Amiodarone and verapamil are the two interactions worth memorising.

questions.prompt: Which class has the strongest mortality benefit in chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?

rationales.a: Consistent mortality reduction across the major trials.
rationales.b: Improve symptoms and congestion but do not reduce mortality.
rationales.c: Reduces hospitalisation without a mortality benefit.

questions.explanation: Symptom control and mortality benefit are different axes — diuretics do the first, not the second.

questions.prompt: Which findings on a 12-lead ECG support left ventricular hypertrophy?

rationales.a: The basis of the Sokolow-Lyon and Cornell criteria.
rationales.b: Lateral ST depression with T inversion accompanies established hypertrophy.

questions.explanation: Voltage plus strain is the classic pairing.

questions.prompt: Which intervention should be withheld until euvolaemia is achieved in decompensated heart failure?

rationales.a: Negative inotropy during congestion can precipitate further decompensation.

questions.explanation: Decongest first, then titrate prognostic therapy.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are appropriate in the first hour of managing acute pulmonary oedema?

rationales.a: Reduces venous return and improves ventilation mechanics immediately.
rationales.b: Produces venodilation early and diuresis shortly after.
rationales.c: Adds volume to an already congested circulation.
rationales.d: Negative inotropy is harmful during acute congestion.
rationales.e: Only indicated with evidence of infection.

questions.explanation: Posture plus diuresis; avoid anything that adds volume or drops contractility.

questions.prompt: Which biomarker result best argues against heart failure in an undifferentiated breathless patient?

rationales.a: A low BNP has a high negative predictive value for heart failure.
rationales.c: Reflects inflammation rather than filling pressure.
rationales.d: Sodium may be normal in established heart failure.

questions.explanation: Left as a draft on purpose: drafts must never surface in the bank or in a quiz.

questions.prompt: Which acid-base disturbance is most typical of aggressive loop diuresis?

rationales.a: Chloride and volume loss drive bicarbonate retention.
rationales.b: Suggests lactate, ketones or toxin accumulation.

questions.explanation: Deliberately attached to no lesson, so it only appears in the unassigned bucket.
